2.text: Sometimes a medium-sized log, or a clumsy wooden implement similar in shape

3.text: to a thick two-pronged fork, is tied to the animal’s neck, though it hinders it

4.text: from grazing properly. The reindeer, secured by the end of the lasso, are

5.text: usually turned out to pasture for a short time daily; but at night the man

6.text: who wants to pasture his animals well will sit up himself, holding the end of

7.text: the rope in his hand, and now and then, while dozing, take a look at his

8.text: reindeer; otherwise they would become entangled, and could not graze at all.

9.text: If well pastured and not overworked, reindeer are swift; and in two days

10.text: a single driver often makes two hundred miles, provided the snow is thin and

11.text: hard, as it usually is on the tundra. The lightest camp makes, on an average,

12.text: twenty-five miles a day; and the large camp, from ten to fifteen miles, though

13.text: often, especially early in the fall, not more than from three to five miles.

14.text: When tired, the reindeer, especially the Chukchee reindeer, must be given

15.text: immediate rest. If compelled to make further effort, it will become quite

16.text: exhausted, and oftentimes drop dead on the spot. Therefore wealthy men

17.text: are always on the look-out to acquire additional harness-reindeer, either for pack-

18.text: sledges or for fast driving, that they may be able to relieve frequently those

19.text: in use. The Chukchee saying is, however, “The poor man’s reindeer are

20.text: more enduring,” compelled as they are to constant exercise. In the reindeer-

21.text: races, the fresh, well-rested reindeer always win; and, to quote another saying,

22.text: “All stakes are taken by the largest breeders.”

23.text: ECONOMICAL VALUE OF REINDEER-BREEDING. — The possession of reindeer-

24.text: herds makes the material life of the nomadic Chukchee more stable, especially

25.text: when compared with the precarious subsistence of most of the fishing and seal-

26.text: hunting tribes in his neighborhood, not excepting even the Russians and the

27.text: Russianized natives. In the Kolyma district, where the white salmon does not

28.text: come from the Arctic Sea in large numbers, and where wild reindeer are

29.text: thinly scattered over a large wilderness, the Reindeer Chukchee, though in

30.text: every other respect inferior to the fisher-folk of the river, play the most

31.text: prominent part in the economic life of the country. The river people depend

32.text: on them for skins and fur clothing; and every spring, when the fish-supply is

33.text: exhausted and the usual famine is at hand, the river inhabitants, one by one,

34.text: drive over the tundra with their dog-teams, carrying with them all the household

35.text: things they can spare, to buy with them such animals as their half-wild nomadic

36.text: friends will sell. Even the officials of the towns of Sredne-Kolymsk and Nishne-

37.text: Kolymsk find themselves obliged to visit the wealthy camps, and urgently beg

38.text: the reindeer-breeders to come nearer to the river with animals for slaughter,

39.text: as otherwise the people of the town and the cossacks will be starved. The

40.text: trade of the country at present is carried on chiefly with the produce of rein-

41.text: deer-breeding, such as fawn-skins, curried leather, etc. The costly peltries,

42.text: before coming to the market, also pass through the hands of the wealthy

43.text: reindeer-breeders, who buy them with slaughter-animals from the Tungus, Lamut,
